blocks.text: Put two fingers on your wrist and count. That regular thump is a muscular pump the size of your fist, working about 70 times a minute, every minute, for your whole life — roughly two and a half billion beats without a single day off.

blocks.markdown:
## The plan of the mammalian heart

The heart is a hollow muscular organ divided lengthways by a **septum** into a right side and a left side that never mix their contents. Each side has two chambers: a thin-walled **atrium** above, which receives blood, and a thick-walled **ventricle** below, which pumps it out.

Imagine it as four rooms. The **right atrium** receives deoxygenated blood from the whole body through the vena cava. It passes down through the **tricuspid valve** into the **right ventricle**, which pumps it through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary vein into the **left atrium**, passes through the **bicuspid (mitral) valve** into the **left ventricle**, and is pumped out through the aorta to the whole body.

The **left ventricle wall is much thicker** than the right, because it must generate enough pressure to drive blood round the entire body, whereas the right ventricle only has to reach the nearby lungs.

blocks.caption: Key blood vessels. Note the two exceptions to the usual rule: the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

blocks.title: Double circulation
blocks.text: A circulatory system in which blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit: once through the pulmonary circulation to the lungs, and once through the systemic circulation to the rest of the body. Mammals and birds have double circulation; fish have single circulation.

blocks.markdown:
### Why double circulation is an advantage

In a fish, blood leaves the heart, passes through the gill capillaries and then travels straight on to the body. Passing through one capillary bed costs a great deal of pressure, so the blood reaching the body tissues is moving slowly.

In a mammal, blood returns to the heart after the lungs and is **re-pressurised** before being sent to the body. High pressure means fast delivery of oxygen and fast removal of carbon dioxide, which supports the high metabolic rate that warm-blooded animals need. The complete separation of the two sides also guarantees that oxygenated and deoxygenated blood never mix.

rows: Very narrow, one red cell wide
blocks.caption: Arteries, veins and capillaries compared

blocks.markdown:
### How the vessels suit their jobs

An **artery** must survive a surge of high-pressure blood at every beat, so its wall has thick layers of muscle and elastic fibres. The elastic fibres stretch during the surge and recoil afterwards, smoothing the flow — this recoil is what you feel as a pulse.

A **vein** carries blood at low pressure, so a thick wall is unnecessary and a wide lumen reduces resistance. Because the pressure is too low to guarantee flow against gravity, veins contain **valves** that shut if blood starts to flow backwards, and the squeezing of nearby skeletal muscles helps push blood along.

A **capillary** exists to exchange materials, so its wall is a single layer of flattened cells. Diffusion distance is minimal, capillaries are extremely numerous, and blood flows slowly through them, all of which favour exchange.

blocks.title: Tracing a red blood cell from the toe to the brain
blocks.prompt: Name, in order, the structures a red blood cell passes through in travelling from a capillary in the toe to a capillary in the brain.

steps.text: Leaving the toe capillary the cell enters a small vein, then larger veins, and finally the inferior vena cava.
The vena cava empties into the right atrium. The atrium contracts and blood passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
The right ventricle contracts, forcing blood past the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary artery, which carries it to the lungs. Here the cell picks up oxygen in an alveolar capillary.
Oxygenated blood returns in the pulmonary vein to the left atrium, then passes through the bicuspid valve into the left ventricle.
The left ventricle contracts powerfully, sending blood through the aorta. The carotid artery branches from the aorta and carries the cell up to the brain, where it enters a brain capillary.

blocks.answer: Toe capillary → vein → vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lung capillary → pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid valve → left ventricle → aorta → carotid artery → brain capillary. The cell passes through the heart twice, which is double circulation.

blocks.title: What valves are for
blocks.text: Every valve in the circulatory system does the same job: it prevents backflow. The tricuspid and bicuspid valves stop blood returning to the atria when the ventricles contract; the semilunar valves at the base of the aorta and pulmonary artery stop blood falling back into the ventricles; valves in veins stop blood sliding back down the limbs.

blocks.title: Two exceptions to memorise
blocks.text: 'Arteries carry oxygenated blood' is only a general rule. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood back. Define arteries and veins by the direction of flow relative to the heart, never by the oxygen content.

points: The heart has four chambers: two atria that receive blood and two ventricles that pump it out.
The left ventricle wall is thickest because it pumps blood to the whole body.
Valves throughout the system prevent the backflow of blood.
Arteries have thick elastic walls and narrow lumens; veins have thinner walls, wide lumens and valves; capillaries are one cell thick for exchange.
Double circulation re-pressurises blood after the lungs, giving fast delivery to the tissues and no mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
